controversies/monothelite-controversy/qu: Does Christ have one will (as one person) or two wills, divine and human (as two natures)?
controversies/monothelite-controversy/ti: The Monothelite controversy: one will or two?
controversies/monothelite-controversy/su: A seventh-century imperial compromise designed to reconcile Miaphysites proposed one ‘energy’ and then one ‘will’ in Christ. Maximus the Confessor and the popes of Rome resisted, at great personal cost; the Third Council of Constantinople (681) defined two natural wills in harmony.
controversies/monothelite-controversy/si: We accept Chalcedon's two natures. But will belongs to the one who wills — the person — and Christ is one person. To speak of two wills is to imagine a human ego set against God inside the Saviour. Confessing one theandric operation and one will protects his unity and can heal the wounds of Chalcedon with our Egyptian and Syrian brethren.
Two wills would imply potential conflict in Christ.
Pope Honorius I himself spoke of ‘one will’.
A nature without a will is incomplete.
Gethsemane shows a human will distinct from the divine.

Will is a property of nature: the Father, Son and Spirit have one will because they share one nature; Christ, having two natures, has two wills. If he did not assume a human will, our will — the very place where Adam fell — remains unhealed. In Gethsemane we see the human will of the Son, in agony, freely bending to the divine. That obedience is our salvation.
Will belongs to nature, not person (the Trinity has three persons and one will).
Matthew 26:39 reveals a human will freely submitting.
Two wills appear to imply two subjects.
controversies/monothelite-controversy/ti: Pact of Union in Alexandria on ‘one theandric energy’.
Lateran Synod under Pope Martin I condemns monothelitism.
Pope Martin I dies in exile in Crimea.
Maximus the Confessor dies in exile after mutilation.
Third Council of Constantinople defines two wills and energies.
controversies/monothelite-controversy/re: Resolved at the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681), which condemned monothelitism and Pope Honorius I. Dyothelitism is held by Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches; Oriental Orthodox churches confess one united will that is both divine and human.
controversies/monothelite-controversy/co: The condemnation of Honorius became a test case in the 1870 debate on papal infallibility.
Maximus' theology of the will shaped Orthodox teaching on synergy and deification.
controversies/what-happens-at-the-lords-: What happens at the Lord’s Supper?
The Eucharistic controversies and the Marburg Colloquy

All Christians celebrate the Supper Jesus instituted, but they disagree on how (or whether) Christ is present in the bread and wine, whether it is a sacrifice and who may preside. The disagreement divided Catholics from Protestants and, at Marburg in 1529, Lutherans from Reformed.

Christ said "this is my body", and he cannot lie. From Ignatius and Justin onward the Church has believed the bread becomes his flesh. We call the change transubstantiation to say that the reality, not the appearance, is changed: Christ is wholly present, to be received and adored, and the one sacrifice of Calvary is made present on our altars.
Literal sense of the words of institution and John 6

The Holy Spirit descends on the gifts and makes them truly the Body and Blood of Christ. We confess the change with the Fathers but do not presume to explain it; the Eucharist is heaven on earth, the Church becoming what it receives.

"This is my body": the words stand firm. We will not explain them away with Zwingli’s "signifies" or with Rome’s philosophy. Christ’s body and blood are truly in, with and under the bread and wine, given to all who eat, for the forgiveness of sins.
Bread and body cannot both be
We truly feed on Christ’s flesh and blood, not by dragging him down into the bread but by being lifted up to him by the Holy Spirit. The signs are not empty: God gives what they signify to faith.

The flesh profits nothing; the Spirit gives life. "Is" here means "signifies", as when Christ says "I am the vine". In the Supper we remember his once-for-all sacrifice, give thanks and pledge ourselves to him as a body; to seek his flesh in bread is to look for the living among the dead.
Justin describes the Eucharist as "not common bread".
Paschasius Radbertus’ On the Body and Blood of the Lord; Ratramnus replies (c.843).
Berengar of Tours forced to swear that Christ’s body is sensibly broken by priests’ hands.
Urban IV institutes the feast of Corpus Christi.
Luther’s Babylonian Captivity attacks transubstantiation and the sacrifice of the Mass.
Marburg Colloquy: Luther and Zwingli fail to agree on the bodily presence.
Augsburg Confession X affirms the true presence.
Consensus Tigurinus unites Calvin and Bullinger.
Lutheran Formula of Concord VII rejects the Reformed view.
Leuenberg Agreement: European Lutheran and Reformed churches declare table fellowship.
WCC’s Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry records broad convergence.
Rome recognises the Anaphora of Addai and Mari of the Assyrian Church of the East.

Partly resolved by dialogue: Lutheran and Reformed churches in Europe (1973) and the US (1997) entered full communion; Catholic–Lutheran and Anglican–Catholic dialogues found substantial agreement on real presence. Yet Catholic, Orthodox, confessional Lutheran and many evangelical churches still do not share communion, and the memorial view predominates among evangelicals.
Prevented a united Protestant front in 1529–30; Zwingli died in battle in 1531 without Lutheran allies.
Shaped distinct liturgies, church architecture and devotional lives.
Remains the most visible sign of Christian division: separate tables.
controversies/who-may-be-ordained/summar: Christian traditions disagree about who may be ordained and by whom: whether valid ordination requires bishops in apostolic succession, and whether women may be ordained as deacons, priests, pastors or bishops. The question has become one of the most divisive in modern church life.
controversies/who-may-be-ordained/sides/: Women may be ordained to all ministries

At Pentecost the Spirit fell on sons and daughters. Paul names women as deacon, co-worker and even apostle, and declares that in Christ there is neither male nor female. The few restrictive verses addressed particular problems, just as Paul’s instructions to slaves did. Two centuries of women preachers, missionaries and pastors show the Spirit’s gifting.
Priesthood reserved to men (Catholic and Orthodox)

Christ, who broke many conventions about women, chose twelve men as apostles, and the Church East and West has never ordained women priests. The priest stands in persona Christi, the Bridegroom, before the Church his bride. This is not a judgement of worth: Mary, the greatest of the saints, was not an apostle.
Women deacons in the early Church

Men and women are equally made in God’s image, but Scripture reserves the office of pastor-elder to qualified men, grounding this in creation, not culture (1 Tim 2:13). Women are gifted for countless ministries, but the eldership is a role of servant headship modelled on Christ.

Ordination is not a congregation’s appointment but Christ’s gift through the apostles and their successors by the laying on of hands. Clement and Irenaeus point to this succession as the guarantee of apostolic faith; without it, the Church’s ministry loses its sacramental link to the apostles.
Bishop and elder identical in NT
controversies/who-may-be-ordained/timeli: 1 Clement describes apostolic appointment of successors.
Chalcedon canon 15 regulates the ordination of deaconesses (minimum age 40).
Quaker Margaret Fell publishes Women’s Speaking Justified.
Antoinette Brown is ordained by a Congregational church in New York.
Leo XIII’s Apostolicae Curae declares Anglican orders invalid.
Florence Li Tim-Oi ordained priest in China, the first in the Anglican Communion.
Inter Insigniores restates Catholic teaching on male priesthood.
Danvers Statement (complementarian) and founding of Christians for Biblical Equality (egalitarian).
Church of England General Synod votes to ordain women priests; Porvoo Agreement shares episcopal succession with Nordic and Baltic Lutherans.
Ordinatio Sacerdotalis; first women priests ordained in the Church of England.
Southern Baptist Convention limits pastoral office to men.
Church of England approves women bishops.
controversies/who-may-be-ordained/resolu: No common resolution. Catholic and Orthodox churches hold male priesthood as unchangeable; most mainline Protestant and many Pentecostal churches ordain women; evangelicals are divided. Disputes over women’s and LGBTQ ordination contributed to realignments such as GAFCON (2008) and the United Methodist schism (2019–2024).
controversies/who-may-be-ordained/conseq: Shapes ecumenical prospects between Catholic/Orthodox and Anglican/Lutheran churches.
Has driven denominational splits and new alignments.
Transformed the composition of clergy in many Protestant churches.
controversies/donatist-controversy/quest: Does an unworthy minister invalidate the sacraments?
controversies/donatist-controversy/summa: After the Great Persecution, North African Christians split over whether bishops who had compromised could validly ordain and baptise. The Donatist church of the martyrs insisted on purity; Augustine and the Catholics replied that Christ is the true minister of every sacrament and that the Church is a mixed body until the judgement.
controversies/donatist-controversy/sides: Our fathers died rather than hand over the Scriptures. How can those who betrayed Christ, or who share communion with betrayers, give the Holy Spirit they have lost? The Church is the spotless bride, the enclosed garden; Cyprian taught us that there is no baptism outside it. We are the Church of the martyrs, persecuted again now by bishops in league with the emperor.

If baptism depended on the holiness of the minister, no one could know they were truly baptised. Peter, Paul or Judas may baptise: it is Christ who baptises. The Church will contain wheat and tares until the harvest; to tear it apart for the sake of purity is to sin against the love that is its very life.
controversies/donatist-controversy/timel: Diocletian’s persecution demands the surrender of Scriptures.
Caecilian consecrated bishop of Carthage; Numidian bishops elect Majorinus.
Constantine’s favour to the Church; a Roman synod under Miltiades finds for Caecilian.
Council of Arles rules against rebaptism and for Caecilian.
Augustine’s On Baptism, against the Donatists.
Conference of Carthage under Marcellinus finds for the Catholics.
Vandal invasion of North Africa overtakes the conflict.
controversies/donatist-controversy/resol: The imperial verdict of 411 and subsequent coercive laws gave the Catholic party legal victory, but Donatist communities survived until the Arab conquest. Theologically, Augustine’s position became the norm for Western Catholic and magisterial Protestant churches.
controversies/donatist-controversy/conse: Established the principle that sacraments are valid regardless of the minister’s worthiness.
Set a precedent for state coercion of dissenting Christians, justified by Augustine.
Weakened North African Christianity before the Vandal and Arab conquests.
